MEDIA ALERT
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

DATE: 27 MAY 2026

TRAFFIC ADVISORY: ROAD CLOSURES AND DISRUPTIONS FOR THE INTERNATIONAL FRIENDLY MATCH BETWEEN BAFANA BAFANA & NICARAGUA AT ORLANDO AMSTEL ARENA 

JOHANNESBURG – The Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department (JMPD) wishes to advise motorists and residents of significant traffic disruptions in Orlando, Soweto, on Friday, 29 May 2026. This is due to the International Friendly fixture between South Africa (Bafana Bafana) and Nicaragua.

To ensure public safety and maintain order, JMPD officers will be deployed at key intersections to facilitate traffic flow around the Orlando Amstel Arena.

Affected Routes & Road Closures

Road closures will be implemented starting from 02:00 PM (14:00). Heavy traffic and closures are expected on the following major routes between 02:00 PM (14:00) and 11:00 PM (23:00):

N17
Soweto Highway
Klipspruit Valley Road
Martha Louw Street
Mooki Street
Sofasonke Street
Kumalo Main Road

Specific Intersections to be Closed:

Mooki Street: Between Nkom Ya Hlaba and Masopha Streets.

Martha Louw Street: Between Klipspruit Valley Road and Mooki Street.

Post-Match Traffic Flow (One-Way Systems)

To expedite the dispersal of fans after the final whistle:

Klipspruit Valley Road will be converted into a one-way street, running from Martha Louw Street towards the N17 traffic circle.

Soweto Highway: Will be closed at Eben Cuyler Street. Vehicles coming from Diepkloof will be diverted to Moshoeshoe Street in Orlando East.

Mooki Street: No left turn from Mooki Street onto Soweto Highway

Alternative Routes & Parking

Alternative Routes:

Drivers are encouraged to use Ballenden and Masopha Streets as alternatives to Mooki Street, or utilise the broader Soweto Highway network where closures are not in effect.

Spectator Parking Locations:

Corner of Martha Louw and Klipspruit Valley Road (Open Space).

Local Schools: Shomane High, AB Xuma Primary (Scott St), Lofentse Girls High (Mooki St), Zithathele Primary (Mooki St), Leratong Primary, Orlando High, Selelekela High (Mooki St), and Lereshe Primary (Adams St).

Orlando Court (Mooki Street).

Note: Parking inside the Orlando Amstel Arena is strictly reserved for VIPs, Media, and VOC members.

Event Logistics

Gates Open: 3:00 PM (15:00)
Kick-off: 6:00 PM (18:00)

JMPD urges spectators to arrive early to avoid gate congestion and requests residents to remain patient during this period. Please plan your routes in advance to minimise delays.

END

Issued by the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department (JMPD) Communications Unit #SaferJoburg #JoburgRoadSafety #JHBTraffic #BafanaBafana #JHBTraffic

🇬🇷⚡🇹🇷 A Learner's Guide for Greek Friends — Long on Opinions, Short on Knowledge — 5

Topic: GEOGRAPHY, 12 NAUTICAL MILES, AND CASE LAW

The Greek thesis likes to speak in numbers. "Twelve miles is our right," "equidistance is the automatic rule," "our coastal length is longer." Numbers look crisp, inferences feel mechanical. As if delimitation were an arithmetic exercise.
Here is the problem: the law of the sea, beneath the numbers, takes geographyand equity into account. Arithmetic alone yields no result; if it did, every maritime boundary dispute in the world would be settled in minutes. They are not — because each case comes with its own geography, its own balance between the parties, its own accumulated jurisprudence.
This thread opens three things against the Greek thesis's number games:
(a) Geography is not outside the law; it is part of it. The Aegean is a semi-enclosed sea; Greece is a mainland state, not an archipelagic one.
(b) Twelve miles is not a right "in every situation"; it is a rule whose consequences must be weighed.
(c) Case law is not the material of the Greek thesis but of its refutation.
First we will dismantle the common slogans; then we will move to the two most sophisticated fronts of the Greek thesis.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: That the Aegean is a semi-enclosed sea does not affect delimitation.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: UNCLOS Article 123 does not draw a boundary on its own — true. But you cannot stretch that into "the geography of the Aegean is irrelevant." Article 123 imposes a duty of cooperation in semi-enclosed seas; and throughout delimitation jurisprudence, principles such as good faith, prohibition of abuse of rights, and cut-off effect feed directly from geography.
You cannot sweep aside the elements that courts repeatedly bring into play by calling them "irrelevant." Geography is not the law's backdrop; it is its ground. To think of the Aegean as if it were the open ocean, you must ignore the rest of the Aegean's map — which is precisely what the architecture of Greek propaganda requires.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Greece can act as an archipelagic state and connect its islands into a single maritime jurisdiction zone.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: No. The archipelagic state is a special category defined in Part IV of UNCLOS: states constituted wholly or principally by archipelagos. Indonesia, the Philippines, the Bahamas. Athens, Thessaloniki, the Peloponnese, Thrace are the body of a mainland state.
Greece is a continental state with islands; it is not an archipelagic state. You cannot link your islands with archipelagic baselines like Indonesia and close off Türkiye. Category jumping is not law. To depict yourselves as an archipelagic state, you would first have to renounce the mainland; will you?
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Our total coastal length is longer, so our share must be larger.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: You obtain that "longer coast" by summing island coasts with full effect. You assume what is in dispute, then derive the conclusion from your own assumption. This is called walking in circles.
The law works the other way around: delimitation first determines which features produce what effect, then proportionality is tested. The Greek thesis reverses the sequence: it sums all island coasts at full effect and then says "look, our total is larger." The result is presented as the cause. This is not legal reasoning; it is a circular argument.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: The 12 nautical mile territorial sea around islands is an unquestionable right.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: UNCLOS Article 3 says "up to 12 miles"; it does not say "12 miles in every sea, regardless of consequences." A reasonable ceiling in the open ocean; in a narrow, semi-enclosed sea like the Aegean, the same rule alone turns the whole sea into Greek internal waters.
The ordinary interpretation of a rule in the open sea can become abuse of rights in a narrow sea. UNCLOS Article 300 forbids precisely this. What is presented as "a right" becomes, when applied without regard to consequences, the place where the right ends. Türkiye's objection is not to the 12-mile concept, but to its balance-destroying application in the Aegean.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: By opposing 12 miles, Türkiye is rejecting the law of the sea itself.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: Türkiye is not rejecting the law of the sea; it is rejecting the abuse of rights. UNCLOS Article 3 says "up to 12 miles"; it does not say "in the Aegean its application is mandatory regardless of consequences." An ordinary rule in the open sea, applied in the Aegean, would trap Türkiye in narrow corridors between territorial-water arcs. The result is not the law's victory but its defeat.
The objection is not to the rule but to the conversion of the rule into a weapon designed to drown a state. UNCLOS itself, through its Article 300, prohibits this. Türkiye may be outside the convention; but the principles underlying the convention are taken at least as seriously by Türkiye as by the parties to it — perhaps more so.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Türkiye's "casus belli" posture on 12 miles is an unlawful threat.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: Casus belli is a state's declaration that a step targeting its vital interests would be considered cause for war; in itself it is not a threat but a structural warning. Türkiye, by the 1995 Grand National Assembly resolution, framed this on the basis of the Aegean's factual geographic reality.
In the Aegean, 12 miles is not an ordinary expansion of the territorial sea; it is the unilateral conversion of roughly 70 percent of the sea into Greek internal waters. To oppose this is not an unlawful threat; it is a legitimate state position deriving from the geography of a semi-enclosed sea. International law allows the prevention of abuse of rights; we are not required to say "please, by all means, take it" in order not to prevent it.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: The equidistance line is the automatic rule of law.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: It is not. The North Sea Continental Shelf Cases (1969) rejected this simplicity half a century ago. The International Court of Justice ruled that equidistance is not a mandatory rule of custom; delimitation is to be carried out on the basis of equitable principles, taking into account all relevant circumstances.
Subsequent jurisprudence reinforced this: Tunisia-Libya (1982), Libya-Malta (1985), Romania-Ukraine (2009), Bangladesh-Myanmar (2012), Nicaragua-Colombia (2012). In each one, mechanical equidistance was either taken as a starting line and then adjusted, or not used at all. Delimitation is the work of equity, not of the ruler.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Modern jurisprudence grants islands half or one-third effect; therefore Türkiye too should give the islands some share.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: No. The Turkish thesis is not a bargaining position derived from case law. The Turkish thesis is this: the Greek islands lying in front of the Anatolian coast have no continental shelf or EEZ entitlement. Case law exists to refute your thesis, not to construct ours.
Outcomes like half effect or third effect are special equity corrections applied by courts in specific geographies. The Turkish thesis is prior to case law and stands above case law: in the Aegean's particular geography, with two main continental states facing each other, islands producing closing-off continental shelf and EEZ contradicts the foundational principles of delimitation law.
So it is not "let us also give you a share" bargaining; it is "let us recognise the category error" refusal. Blurring this distinction is the final barricade of the Greek thesis.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Courts always rule in favour of islands — you cite only exceptions.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: What you call "exceptions" are now widespread enough to constitute the rule:
Channel Islands enclaved (1977).
Snake Island could not determine the      delimitation (2009).
St. Pierre and Miquelon confined to a      "keyhole" (1992).
Kerkennah awarded half effect (1982,      Tunisia-Libya).
Malta — an independent island state —      pushed back against Libya (1985).
St. Martin's received territorial waters, no      EEZ (2012).
Itu Aba classified as a      "rock," generated no full EEZ (2016).
Philippines-China Arbitration (2016) reclassified most Spratly      features as "rocks."
When seven or eight "exceptions" pile up, what you have is not an exception but a line. Show one modern judgment granting an island automatic full effect — you cannot.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Greece is the natural owner of the Aegean; geography says so.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: Geography says exactly the opposite. The eastern coast of the Aegean is Türkiye from end to end. To erase that, you would have to cut a continent in half. This sea is Türkiye's geography, its economy, its maritime traffic, its security.
The visual cleverness of the Greek thesis is this: presenting the island chain as a "barrier" and keeping Anatolia at arm's length from the Aegean. But the barrier is not a geographic fact; it is an intent placed at the margin of the map. Geography, read plainly, shows: two main continental states with a semi-enclosed sea between them. Greek islands do not change the geographic reality of that sea; they only complicate the delimitation question.
🔻 So far we have dismantled the common slogans of the Greek thesis. Two harder fronts remain: sophisticated framings advanced at academic level. The strongest cards in the Greek hand — we come to them now. 🔻
🇬🇷 CLAIM: The Aegean is not a "grey sea." Greek islands have maritime jurisdiction zones; Türkiye can only press claims outside Greek territorial waters and only in the narrow areas where continental shelf or EEZ claims actually overlap. "The Aegean is not a Greek lake" is an empty slogan; law is not made by slogans.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: This is the most sophisticated version of the Greek thesis — and the most cunning. Because the heart of the argument rests on a hidden premise: "The initial maritime jurisdiction zones of the Greek islands have already been established; the debate is confined to a narrow overlap corridor." That is precisely what is contested.
Türkiye is not constructing a thesis in which "the existence of the islands has been erased." The Turkish thesis says this: the Greek islands lying in front of the Anatolian coast lack the capacity to generatecontinental shelf and EEZ in a manner that closes off Türkiye's mainland projection. This is not erasure of the islands from the map; it is the concrete application of the prohibition of cut-off effect in delimitation law.
The sentence "let us speak only of the narrow overlap zone" skips the question of who determines where that overlap begins and ends. If you grant the islands full initial effect by presumption, the overlap area emerges as a thin sliver; Anatolia is already closed off from the sea. The real question of the Turkish thesis is precisely this: the area of overlap is the consequence of the islands' capacity debate, not its premise.
"The Aegean is not a Greek lake" may sound like a slogan; but the legal content underneath is this: in a semi-enclosed sea where two main continental states face each other, the production of closing-off full effect by islands contradicts the foundational principles of delimitation law. This is not a slogan — it is a category question. The sophisticated Greek version is also trying to close that category in advance — only in more refined language.
🇬🇷 CLAIM: Türkiye is not a party to UNCLOS, yet it appropriates the concepts of "equity," "abuse of rights," and "semi-enclosed sea." It rejects the core rules of the Convention — the 12 miles of Article 3 and the initial effect Article 121 grants to islands. A country that lost the votes and refused to sign cannot dictate the correct interpretation of UNCLOS. Article 121 is clear: islands generate maritime jurisdiction; the only debate is how much effect they receive at the boundary. Article 3 is clear: a coastal state has the right to up to 12 miles of territorial sea; when a coastal state chooses 12 miles, that is not an abuse of rights. When opposite coasts overlap, what is required is not veto, but delimitation.
🇹🇷 ANSWER: The strongest front of the Greek thesis. Let us unpack each sentence.
On the "cherry-picking" charge: The concepts of equity, abuse of rights, and semi-enclosed sea are not unique to UNCLOS. In the ICJ's North Sea Continental Shelf Cases (1969), Tunisia-Libya (1982), Libya-Malta (1985), Romania-Ukraine (2009), these concepts are established as parts of customary international law. Türkiye is not selecting from UNCLOS; it relies on customary principles that exist prior to and independent ofUNCLOS. Rejecting the convention does not entail rejecting the custom that lies beneath it. Whoever argues otherwise is conflating the legal architecture.
On "you lost the votes, you cannot dictate" charge: At UNCLOS III, Türkiye did not lose a vote — it placed its position on the record openly, continuously, and consistently. That is the textbook definition of the persistent objectordoctrine. The ICJ's Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries Case (1951) recognises this status explicitly. Türkiye is not dictating interpretation; it is preserving its doctrinal status of non-attachment to a rule. Two different things.
On "Article 121 is clear, islands generate zones": Article 121(3) is equally clear: rocks that cannot sustain human habitation or economic life of their own generate no EEZ or continental shelf. Moreover, 121(2) regulates an island's capacity; it does not automatically guarantee full effect in delimitation. The sentence "the only debate is how much effect they receive at the boundary" belatedly accepts what jurisprudence has said for a century — but misses the Turkish thesis: in the Aegean's particular geography, full closing-off effect is categorically impossible.
On "12 miles is not abuse of rights": Abuse of rights looks not at the abstract existence of a rule, but at the concrete outcome of its application. The same 12 miles is an ordinary right in the open ocean; in the Aegean it means the unilateral conversion of roughly 70 percent of the sea into Greek internal waters. UNCLOS itself, through Article 300, prohibits this. To read "12 miles is a right" as "applies without consequence in every situation" is the definition of abuse of rights.
On "delimitation, not veto": Türkiye is not against delimitation; it is against your maximalist map being imposed as the starting point of delimitation. In the Black Sea, boundaries were drawn with Bulgaria, Romania, and Ukraine — by treaty, by negotiation, by reasonable reading of overlapping coasts. This is not happening in the Aegean because Athens insists on its own map, not on geography, as the starting point. Who is vetoing? The side that makes its own maximalist reading, rather than geography, the precondition.
Conclusion: This argument's strength comes not from its legal content but from its sophisticated presentation. Strip away the legal varnish, and what appears is the same old sentence: "We will not yield our claims; you submit." Only in more academic language.
Summary:
Geography is part of the law, not outside it. Twelve miles is not an automatic right in every situation; it is a ceiling whose consequences must be weighed. Equidistance is not an automatic rule; half a century of jurisprudence rejected that. Courts do not always grant islands full effect.
The sophisticated Greek arguments also try to cover up the same category question — only in more refined language. The "narrow overlap zone" framing is a manoeuvre to pre-establish the islands' initial effect; the "cherry-picking" charge is an attempt to compress customary law inside UNCLOS.
Türkiye is not stacking numbers against numbers; it preserves the fundamental logic of the law that rests on geography, equity, and the prohibition of cut-off effect. The ruler does not produce law; every line drawn must respect actual geography.
Next chapter: Kastellorizo (Meis) and the Eastern Mediterranean. How a feature 600 kilometres from mainland Greece was meant to be converted into tens of thousands of square kilometres of EEZ — and why the answer to that, on legal and geographic grounds alike, is simple.
